newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: MANUFACTURERS URGE ACTION PLAN FOR INDUSTRY
Australia's manufacturers have called on the Federal Government to help reverse a long-term decline in their sector.
The Australian Chamber of Manufactures says manufacturing's share of the economy and jobs has fallen from 24 per cent in 1970 to 14-point-seven per cent.
The Chamber wants to see a 40 per cent rise in exports, an average of at least three per cent in annual manufacturing growth and a rise in investment to at least 20 per cent.
The targets are contained in an Action Plan the manufacturers' peak body has put to the Mortimer Review of Australia's Business Programs.
AUSSIE HOUSES FOR JAPAN
Houses have become Australia's fastest growing export to Japan.
The Australian Trade Commission says an Australian-made home is about 20 per cent cheaper than the equivalent from a typical Japanese builder.
Austrade's executive general manager for North Asia, Greg Dodds, says he expects exports of housing materials and services to Japan to earn around 120-million dollars this year.
Japan has been Australia's biggest export market since 1969, but largely based on commodities.
GOVERNMENT ACCUSED OF "SCIENTIFIC MCCARTHYISM"
Scientist Dr Paul Komesaroff says Federal Cabinet's decision to dump Professor John Funder from a top Government science appointment is "scientific McCarthyism".
Professor Funder was offered the job to head the National Health and Medical Research Council by Health minister, Michael Wooldridge, but Cabinet's rejected the proposal.
It's been widely reported Independent Senator Brian Haradine opposed the appointment, mainly because Professor Funder supported use of the abortion drug R-U-4 8-6.

Dr Komesaroff, of Melbourne's Eleanor Shaw Centre for the Study of Medicine, Society and Law, has told ABC Radio there's a great deal of concern about the decision in the scientific and ethical community.
He says there's also alarm about the possibility that a precedent may have been set in which religious, political and ethical tests are applied to individuals before they take up public appointments.
COUNCIL SAYS KERIN DECISION "EXTRAORDINARY"
The Cattle Council of Australia has described as extraordinary, the Federal Government's decision not to extend the appointment of John Kerin as head of the Meat and Livestock Corporation.
The Council, as well as industry, wanted the former Labor minister to remain at the Corporation's helm pending its restructure.
But Federal Cabinet's rejected the plan, and Primary Industries Minister John Anderson, who's believed to have supported the extenion, has shrugged off the decision.
Mr Anderson says it's not a serious problem because the industry will have a totally new structure within weeks.
But the Cattle Council's Justin Toohey, says it's a difficult and crucial time for the industry, which can't be left rudderless.
ACT GOVERNMENT TO HAVE POSITION ON EUTHANASIA
The A-C-T's Legislative Assembly will make its position known on voluntary euthanasia, as early as next week.
Independent Michael Moore will introduce the bill to the parliament today, and says there's general agreement the Assembly should make an in-principle decision on it next Wednesday.
An in-principle vote in favour of the bill would allow the Assembly to register its position, before Federal Parliament votes on the Kevin Andrews bill.
That bill is aimed at over-riding the Northern Territory's voluntary euthanasia law.
Mr Moore says detailed debate could wait until later in the year.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
